utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just having in mind our pretty tight schedule today, I spoke with the Prosecution, and we agreed that the associated exhibits for this witness would be dealt in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no problem as far as the Chamber is concerned to do it in writing. Any other matter? If not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony, and I would urge you again to make -- take a breath between question and answer and try to speak not too quickly. Mr. Ivetic will give the good example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I would like to now ask you about some of the tactics that you witnessed of the Bosnian Presidency forces, and first of all am I correct that on several occasions you, that is to say the UNMO mission, had to complain to the Presidency forces to move their mortars because they were too close to UN buildings or facilities?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at paragraph 20 of your statement, P503, and that's page 15 of the same, you talk of instances where the Bosnian Presidency forces appeared to be firing at the Serbs trying to draw the Serbs to counter-fire or retaliate. In those instances would you consider it plausible or reasonable that a local artillery commander on the Bosnian Serb side would have the level of autonomy to be able to respond on his own to such an attack without seeking the approval of superiors?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we can briefly turn to --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could briefly turn to 1D424, and, sir, this is the transcript from your testimony in the Karadzic proceedings, and if we could turn to page 5 of this 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to make life easier for those coming after us, page 2, line 12, paragraph 20 is at page 5. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus in on lines 16 through 18, and here, sir, you are talking about the Bosnian Serb artillery, and you say: "So not only were they firing on a target that we couldn't identify as being military, but they couldn't even analyse what they had done." Am I understanding your terminology to mean that the Serb artillery could not visually confirm where their shot had fallen and what their fire had accomplished vis-a-vis the target?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during direct, counsel asked you about the time period pre-dating the Markale shelling. I'd like to ask you in relation to the Markale 1 shelling, which occurred on the 5th of February, 1994, am I correct that it was your view that the investigation was inconclusive, that is to say it could not be established to a reasonable degree of certainty which side fired that fateful round?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on those documents that I have seen, and I don't know whether I've seen them all, that is still my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Am I also correct that you have knowledge of another incident that sticks in -- that's significant where a civilian appeared to have been killed on the airport road at the junction with the Dobrinja road by sniper where the -- where there was a CNN media crew nearby?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That incident was based on our judgement though. There was never any proof. The only possible reason that we could see was because a CNN convoy passed by within minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question is still very factual. Was there an incident where a CNN crew was nearby? That's the only thing. Why they were there, by -- for whatever reason, that's not part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. I didn't answer it correctly, Your Honour. Yes, the CNN crew passed by. They were not in the neighbourhood. They passed by within minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up number -- I apologise. Just waiting for the B/C/S translation to catch up. I would like to call up number 1D00433 in e-court and turn to page 21 in the English and page 26 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, this is an unredacted copy of the statement that you have hopefully still in front of you, but you won't see this text. It was redacted in that version. This is paragraph number 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that Mr. Registrar has difficulty with this number. Could you please verify, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D00433. And if we could then turn to page 21 in the English and 26 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we're looking at then paragraph 92. And for purposes of the record, I'll read the paragraph in its entirety before asking you my follow-up questions: "In mid-December 1993, I participated in an investigation of attacks by Bosnian soldiers on several Serb villages near Han Pijesak. I observed freshly burned houses and witness accounts indicated that all who were caught were killed (0055-2665-0055-2665 is a report regarding this incident). I believe this was done by the Bosnians to show the Bosnian Serbs that they had limited troops and could not protect everyone. I learned from an intelligence source aerial surveillance showed that from October 1993 onwards there was a pattern of villages destroyed in the same manner." First of all, Mr. Thomas, could you affirm that this paragraph of your redacted statement is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and if asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers on this topic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to now clarify. The pattern of villages destroyed in the same manner, would those also have been ethnic Serb villages presumed destroyed by Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I couldn't tell from the intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court 65 ter 28527. And while we wait for this, I believe it is a report dated the 19th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I could direct your attention to the English version. Do you recognise this document as the report that resulted from your investigation into the destroyed village referred to in paragraph 92 of your unredacted statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the middle of the page. We see a number of other villages listed where it was alleged that similar things happened. Do you know if these are the villages that are referenced in the surveillance that showed about the affected territory?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any investigations or formal complaints were undertaken by either UNPROFOR or the UNMO mission relating to the actions of the Presidency forces in any of these villages?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No action was taken because we received no further complaints from the Bosnian Serbs about these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document, number 28527, as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It becomes Exhibit D102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D102 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, by the way what I think I intervened in a relatively early stage in the examination-in-chief to ask for the basis for some of the observations by this witness. Of course what the witness believes to be the case also may need some factual basis. If you want to explore that, that might assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please elaborate on how you came to the belief that these villages were, in fact, destroyed by the Bosnian Presidency forces and your belief that they wanted to show the Bosnian Serbs that they could not protect everyone?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first investigation was made on the only request made by the Serbs to conduct an investigation. I was not satisfied that that was the only occasion. I waited for a Serb -- follow-up Serb complaint. None was received. I check with a NATO intelligence source. I was verbally told that there were sufficient grounds to think that there had been other villages, a belt of villages, that showed up as hot spots, and that's all he would tell me. And I moved some Serbo-Croatian speaking military observers towards the area Pale and looked at getting accommodation so they could conduct investigations, and you have the result of my report. But no further complaints were ever received, or, no further requests for investigations were ever received. I passed this report to my superiors in Zagreb, and they never directed that I conduct further investigations either. In fact, they considered that by deploying people to that area and a special team being prepared was a waste of my resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, to -- I think I can understand what you said to be in support of these attacks having been made by the Bosnians, also of a certain pattern. At least there's -- I can imagine that you would use this information as support for that, but I still have difficulties in understanding how what you told us could be a factual basis for the -- your belief that it was done to show the Bosnian Serbs that they had limited troops and could not protect everyone, that that was the thought behind these attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was quite surprised at the -- professionally surprised at the ability of the Bosnian forces to have come 200 kilometres, because these forces did not originate in Sarajevo, to have come almost 200 kilometres into -- within 20 kilometres of the major Serb -- Bosnian Serb headquarters and completely destroy a village with a large party of men and then drive the cattle off, quite a large herd of cattle off in the direction of Bijelvo Selo [phoen]. I cannot believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems it's your logic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which leads you to this conclusion as the purpose of the exercise. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at your amalgamated statement again, P503, and focus on paragraph the 99 of the same, which will be found on page 31 in the English and page 38 in the B/C/S. While we wait for that, I will advise that here you are talking about the large amount of equipment the Bosnian Presidency forces had in the Kosevo tunnel and that this tunnel was therefore turned into a weapons collection point. Can you enlighten us on what kind of equipment you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's an earlier document that was submitted as evidence that detailed the sitrep I received, the intelligence analysis I received, such as it was, intelligence, when I took over the job. So any equipment that we had not been able to see was found in the tunnel, and you can just look at the list of equipment that's on that other document and guess that most of that equipment was found in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you identify for us where this particular tunnel is located and if it is in addition to the two tunnels that were discussed yesterday or if it's one and the same?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a road tunnel that's found in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it distinct from the two tunnels that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most definitely. Those were on the front line -- or one was under the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your mission have information about the use of the Tuzla airport by the Bosnian Presidency forces to transport guns and personnel and ammunition into the Bosnian Muslim enclaves of Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. That was outside my area of responsibility and I had enough to do in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last question for you, sir, just to be clear. In the course of your time as the SMO in Sarajevo, you never personally witnessed General Mladic giving orders for combat to any units of the Bosnian Serb Army, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Ms. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning. The tunnel that you were just referring to, the road tunnel, the Kosevo tunnel, could you tell me whether that was ever the subject of artillery bombardment by the Bosnian Serb Army during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure. That general area received hits, but it was not a specific target that we could determine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was it ever struck so that the actual tunnel collapsed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was there ever concentrated fire in that area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there never was concentrated fire on almost any area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked a few minutes ago about a report you prepared on an investigation in the area of a village called Pocolovaka [phoen], and my question is: How much villages did you actually physically visit to investigate the allegations of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only visited one area in particular, and we received information on the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The aerial information that you received, could it assist you in determining who had been responsible for any damage that you could see from the aerial photos?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get to see the aerial photos. This individual -- I was not privy to this particular information. The individual gave did to me to assist me in indicating that there had been activity in those areas, but there was no further -- we needed to investigate on the ground. We did not have the evidence we needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And so in terms of, for example, speaking to survivors of these alleged attacks, did you ever have that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the one village we did visit, there were no survivors that we could talk to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So was -- the incidents with respect to the other villages, were they ever UNMO confirmed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the incident my friend was asking about involving somebody being killed by a sniper and CNN passing by shortly thereafter, was there ever any determination as to who was responsible for killing that civilian?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've also indicated here today that in respect of the Markale 1 or February 5th, 1994, incident, that your opinion is based on the documents you've seen, and you don't know whether you have seen them all. Have you ever seen any expert reports in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I -- well, depends on the definition of "expert."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton. Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there are some adjudicated facts as to the source of fire on the 5th of February, 1994. I was already slightly surprised, if I may say so, that Mr. Ivetic asked the witness whether on the basis of the report at that time had a certain opinion. Two questions: The first the basis for that opinion would be limited to what existed in that year; second, whether the witness is sufficiently qualified to evaluate all those reports. And now before we go on to further explore what one could conclude if one would have only available the material at that time, whether that assists the Chamber is highly unlikely. I mean, if it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would have been thoroughly dealt with by Mr. Ivetic I can imagine that you want to put further questions. But the only thing Mr. Ivetic asked is, Looking at the reports at that time, do you still believe and is that still your conclusion. I can tell you one thing for certain, that the Chamber will not stop at that time in evaluating information available on this incident. Please proceed. And whether the witness has seen any later reports, yes or no, and what his beliefs are or what his opinions are, if he's not an expert, seems to be of low relevance and low probative value.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate the Trial Chamber's direction on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could just go back to a few issues from your testimony yesterday, sir. If you would just bear with me while I put on my glasses. Yesterday during examination, you were read an excerpt of -- in which you had been discussing the Swiss model and the issue of Yugoslav Territorial Defence units. Do you recall that line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And part of what you were asked about was the idea that the Territorial Defence had depots or storage facilities where they would have kept ammunition, for example.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to what actually happened to anything that would have been stored in those depots when the hostilities broke out in Yugoslavia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. It would have been issued out before my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you have actually any personal knowledge of there being ammunition depots within the city of Sarajevo, held by the Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked the following questions and answers yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I had only the temporary transcript available. I don't know if that's a complete transcript available, but I'll read from page 51 of the temporary transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is what you were asked, starting at line 5, and this is -- the question that was asked to you was: "Q. Did you have occasion in Gorazde to have the Kopaca," then unintelligible or unintelligible location identified for you, "... which was the reserve rear command of the SFRY high command, a significant bunker and command structure." You said: "No. "Q. Would such structures, if they existed, be legitimate military targets for an opposing force? "A. Yes, and if Your Honour would give me the caveat. If it was known, so widely known, why was it not shelled ... before I got there." And my question for you is: Was the SFRY a party to the conflict in Bosnia when you were there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have to explain that acronym to me, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It would be the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- the Bosnian Serb government -- I mean the Serbian government was not a party in Yugoslavia when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At page 56 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked some questions about a tunnel that you described as being dug from the front lines on Bosnian Presidency territory towards the Serb front lines, and you indicated in your response to Mr. Ivetic's question at the bottom of page 55, he asked you: "And first of all, perhaps it's best for the witness to confirm. Am I correct that this is a different tunnel," it should say, "than the one that was under the airport?" And you said: "Absolutely. This was as I stated in my earlier testimony, the Serbs accused the Bosnians of making tunnels towards their front lines and the -- this is one of the excuses they used for sniper fire." At whom were they firing and using it as an excuse?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be sniper fire on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was it ever used as an excuse for sniper fire at -- at civilian targets, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At pages 58 and 59 of -- or 59 of the transcript yesterday, you were asked about troop movements for the Bosnian Serb forces, the rotation of troops, and you were asked if you would agree that the Bosnian Presidency forces in Sarajevo had to be moved from more interior positions towards the front lines. Could you tell me whether the Bosnian Presidency forces had available to them motorised -- enough motorised vehicle to move troops to the front line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. In fact, they never used motorised transport to move their troops to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And so how would their troops reach the front line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By walking, and that would mean they would be close to the front lines to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was there ever an occasion when you saw a large group or a large body, for example, of soldiers moving towards the front line from, say, the very centre of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was caught up in a column of soldiers moving -- of people in civilian dress moving to the front line with no weapons, no equipment, who were going to presumably acquire that when they got to the front line, and I was surprised that we weren't subjected to shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So these were unarmed soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were unarmed males, and I can only imagine they were moving to the front to replace people that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There were some questions about French kit which was described as uniform and equipment yesterday. What pieces of equipment were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily the helmet and the flak jacket. And the flak jacket I can only identify when I got closer to the body of men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were also asked yesterday if you would agree with the proposition there were approximately 25.000 armed Bosnian Presidency soldiers that were located in Sarajevo as part of the 1st Corps. First of all, could you tell me if you know what percentage of the 25.000 would be on the front lines at any one time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you receive -- I'm sorry. I'm going too fast, I think. Did you receive any -- or can you recall if you received any intelligence information about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN didn't engage in really intelligence information, and we weren't tasked to acquire intelligence information. So I'm basing my agreement yesterday of 25.000, because that's what I was given in my report that I received on taking command.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could have -- you're referring to the report as part of your briefing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 28558, please. It would be page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the middle of this document here is an indication that it was estimated the Bosnians have approximately 25.000 men in the arms in Sarajevo, out of which a third are permanently on the front line. And if we could scroll to the top of this document, please. This document's called "Description warring factions." Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kind lip not overlap for the sake of interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was this one of the documents that you received at the time of your briefing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You'll note my initial on the top, and that was there before all the documentation stamps were put on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Further -- at the very bottom of the page as it's displayed in English it says, and I don't need it to be moved, it's difficult -- this is with respect to the Bosnian weaponries, it's difficult to get exact numbers of heavy weapons, but an estimation, Bosnians have five tanks, 10 to 15 armoured vehicles, and up to 50 artillery and mortar weapons which they do not have the ammunition. You were referring earlier today about some information you received or about, sorry, weapons that you saw in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw the weapons in the tunnel after the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yesterday you were also asked some questions about civilians, and you were asked if civilians including women and elderly and kids wore uniforms or partial uniforms, and you said yes. What did you mean when you said they were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the aid that was received from other European countries included cast-off uniforms. For example, a popular uniform that was there was the German uniform. They had bits and pieces of old uniforms. And I suppose they had uniforms as well from the -- their relatives that were in the forces who might have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you then were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, let's wait for the translation to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were then asked, sir, if you agreed that such a situation could cause a degree of confusion in identifying combatants, and you said no. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because generally the women and children were easily identifiable as women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions yesterday at page 62 and 63 of the temporary transcript about shelling of -- by Croatian forces in Kiseljak that landed inside the Papa side of Sarajevo, and you responded to that question at the top of page 63: "No. It wasn't UNMO confirmed. The only reason that we suspected is the calibre of round was different, and also there were reports of French guns that were owned by the Croatians in Kiseljak firing ... we made a correlation between the two ... so those why we maintained suspected." And subsequently on page 64 on the same subject, you said -- you referred to this as this particular incident. Was there more than one occasion or only one occasion when you had reason to suspect because of the calibre of round being different that the shelling came possibly from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one occasion that it was brought to my attention, but when we asked the UNPROFOR headquarters, they said that this wasn't the first -- the only occasion that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was the calibre of round?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a medium artillery, and again we can't confirm because we didn't have anybody there, but there were some medium artillery pieces that we were -- that professionally we were interested in, in the area of Kiseljak which were suspected to be of French origin, sold to some Croatians by the French or supplied.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are there differences in the size of calibres of rounds used by French forces than by the forces in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO standard is 155. The Russian standard is 152 for medium guns. And I could be wrong, but all the medium guns that I saw on the JNA -- or provided by the Bosnians to the Bosnian Serbs were 152 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked at pages 79 and 80 of the temporary transcript yesterday about a disagreement you had with General Soubirou on one occasion where he seemed inclined to accept information provided to him by the Bosnian government over information provided to him by one of your UNMOs, and you subsequently indicated in response to questionings about how often this had occurred, and your answer was none. No other occasions "I can recall right now. The only one I recall was the exact opposite of the case you just presented." By exact opposite, do I take it to mean there was an occasion when General Soubirou seemed to -- inclined to accept information provided by the Bosnian Serb side over information from your UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't -- it doesn't involve General Soubirou. It involves General Rose. My observers considered that weapons battery -- a battery of the Bosnian Serb certainly was inside the 20-kilometre zone and General Rose disagreed, but I insisted that my guy was right and I would accept his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On the topic of General Rose, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you, what then is the -- is the opposite that General Rose followed your advice or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They discovered then that we didn't have agreement on where the actual centre of the radius of the 20-kilometre zone was, and that was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How -- I have difficulties understanding how this is the opposite of the other example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it involved a Serbian complaint that we were -- that this gun position was not inside the inclusion zone, and it was -- and involved a different general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I therefore understand that the opposite was that it was related to the opposite party --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where a similar discussion took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were read a passage yesterday -- or a couple passages from a statement provided by General Rose, one of which suggested in which one -- in one of which General Rose suggested that he believed Ganic had organised his secret police to snipe trams. And you went on to say you had no knowledge of that. You were then asked if you had visited a Bosnian Presidency position which was under the control of the police rather than the army. You said you had. And I just wanted to be clear. The -- when you talk about the police, and my friend talked about Ganic's secret police, are we talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we definitely aren't. These people wore uniforms, and I can add that they were nowhere near the trams.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And they wore police uniforms or military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were also read a portion of General Rose's statement where he was critical of the UNMOs, and I just want to continue reading where my friend left off yesterday. He read a portion that - I'll read the last sentence or two - said, the UNMOs: "Many were not technically competent and some were sold out. They were captured by the ones they were -- they were ... with." It continues to say: "They were UNMOs at Pale and Belgrade. I am unaware of whether there were UNMOs based at Lukavica -- Lukavica. I guess the Belgrade ones were monitoring the airport. They were not under my command." You told us earlier in your evidence about your UNMOs being held technically hostage at Lukavica Barracks in April 1994. Was General Rose in command in April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you make him aware of that incident?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was aware of that incident. He was also aware that I had 50 people on the Serb side, including my headquarters for the Lima team in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Page 87 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested to you that, starting at lines 12, by Mr. Ivetic: "Would you agree with me, sir, that due to the manner in which the observation locations were set I -- that on the Serb side of the confrontation line the casualties were not adequately covered by the reports." And you responded --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters while reading. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "A. I would agree." In order for the UN to confirm a casualty on either side of the confrontation line, so a death or a wounding, what did your protocol require?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our protocol required us to go and see the body and the injured person, to visit them in hospital or to go to the morgue, and we visited the morgue in Sarajevo every night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you given free access to hospitals or morgues on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only occasion I recall that we got access to a hospital was when we brought a wounded Serb soldier into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The final area I want to ask you about is the questioning yesterday about UNMO involvement in humanitarian aid escorts. Now, in your answers yesterday, you indicated -- you were asked questions about how often the UNMOs were called upon to facilitate this task, and I want to just make sure I understand your evidence. You mentioned that humanitarian aid agencies would come to headquarters and ask for information. How often did that occur?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did that affect your ability to man your observation posts?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were welcomed in my operations room, and they got the same briefing we accorded General Soubirou or any other visitor to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of whether -- or how frequently UNMOs were actually involved in escorting convoys, how often would that occur?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would happen as rarely as possible. We did it in the case of Gorazde when we had to. And I'm afraid, I admit it, when other humanitarian assistance area that we were involved in, almost a daily basis, and that was in the Zepa pocket where the UN representative was only there four months of the nine months in Sarajevo and the senior military observer in Zepa had to assume the responsibilities to represent the UN in all humanitarian activities including distribution of money and fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was it -- did it affect your ability to have sufficient men or women to man your observation posts in Sarajevo and perform the monitoring of incoming and outgoing fire by needing to escort humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not happy with the use of the word "escort." They basically wanted information, and, yes, I had to take a military observer and assign him to the job of liaison to non-governmental agencies and to UNHCR and aid agencies strictly for liaison on a 24 and 7 duty roster. So I lost one military observer to do that job full time, and that's a job I created in my time based on the amount of work we had to do liaising, providing information. And I would ask you to remember that we were the only UNPROFOR element on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, the Chamber wonders where we are at this moment in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am at the last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In questioning about a document yesterday regarding the delivery of aid, you were asked about if there were incidents where notwithstanding the Serbs agreeing to the delivery of aid it couldn't be done because of other issues involving, for example, the drivers, the absence of a particular kind of ambulance. My question is: Were there occasions when the Serbs didn't agree to the delivery of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those all of my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a small number of questions for you. I suggest that we try to finish before the break. Would you give us an indication, Mr. Ivetic, as on the basis of the re-examination how much time you'd need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None for me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, you told us about the tunnel or the tunnel system in the Nedzarici area. I'm afraid I did not fully explain -- understand what you said. You said the Serbs accused the Bosnians of making tunnels toward their front lines, and this is one of the excuses they used for sniping fire. Now, if I use sniper fire to hit soldiers in tunnels moving to the front lines, wherefore do I need an excuse? Isn't that fully legitimate in military terms?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wouldn't see these soldiers. These soldiers are tunneling, and they're underground, and they were working their way in tunnels towards the Serb lines, and the Serbs couldn't see them. They could just hear them. And so what they did to try and discourage this was to fire at the people that they saw above the area they thought was being tunneled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, therefore, whether they were firing at civilians or not, you wouldn't know because -- who were above the tunnels, or would you know?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in our case we never considered those -- that was the confrontation area, and we weren't considering the people there to be civilians at all. So they wouldn't appear on our sniper casualties as civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If these people moving on the surface not in the tunnels were considered to be military combatants, why would you need an excuse to fire at them? Wouldn't that be totally legitimate?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a cease-fire in place. They didn't -- neither side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's try now to analyse clearly. Were they seeking an excuse for firing during a cease-fire which has got nothing to do with tunnels because that would be irrespective of a tunnel or a -- whatever, or were they seeking to have an excuse for firing at people which were on the ground above where there was a suspicion or it was established that tunnels were dug?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were trying -- they were in violation of the cease-fire, and the -- and the cease-fire, the Bosnians were in violation of the cease-fire by improving their fortifications or preparing for assaults from underground. So both sides were in violation, and we were trying to find the trenches which were a violation -- the tunnels, these small tunnels or infantry tunnels. And we were trying to discourage the sniper fire on the front line which was killing people in violation of the cease-fire. Military people were dying, but not -- but still in violation of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I now better understand your -- what it was about. I have no further questions for you. Still the same, Mr. Ivetic? Mr. Thomas, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and having answered, even very quickly answered, all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour I'm sorry I showed any disrespect to the Bench yesterday, and I apologise to the interpreters and staff for being a little -- talking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there's one matter remaining. Somewhere in your early answers you said you would like to add something, and then I said at the very end of your testimony you could add if there was something you really think was missing which we should know. I'm not inviting you now to deliver a speech, but if there's any specific fact which you had in mind at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was one correction to make sure that something that was said by the Prosecution, it came up on the display as freedom of something, and it wasn't freedom of movement, but I hope that will be corrected in the -- when it's -- and also I'd like to thank the people involved in the process for doing this, because I think it -- as we were -- as a good friend had served three years in -- three different tours in Yugoslavia said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could discourage you from expressing your feelings about the work of this Tribunal and for whom it is good and for whom it is not good. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire whether the next witness is ready after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the witness will be taken by Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jeremy. Interpretation is in place as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours, Danish interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break and resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the -- no. Perhaps the witness could be escorted into the courtroom, and meanwhile, I use the opportunity to inform the Prosecution that the practical consequences of the decision of the Chamber still to be given on the 92 ter motion for Witness RM046, that the practical consequences will be that the witness cannot be called next week. Mr. Groome, we thought it best to inform you immediately about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought into the courtroom perhaps I can mention the three adjudicated facts relevant to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: They are as follows: 767, 768, and 769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I invite you to stand. Yes. Could someone fetch the glasses of the witness. First of all -- good morning, Witness. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. I was informed that you are willing to make that solemn declaration in the English language. Could I invite you to stand and to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. or Mrs., I do not know how to address you, Ms. or Mrs. Weiss. But ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Mrs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, you will first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution, and you will find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Weiss.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In a few sentences could you please provide an outline of your professional background.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I am a trained journalist, and I supplemented that education with studies of literature at Copenhagen university. I was a member of the Danish parliament for 25 years, which I served as a minister for eight years, having different ministerial posts. I was a deputy chair of the Social Democratic Party for 12 years, and in 2001, I decided to leave politics and go back to my original profession as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: What are you currently doing now?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Currently I work as a literary critic and reviewer for a Danish newspaper called "Weekendavisen," and in addition to that, I occasionally write reports from various places in the world for the same newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mention that you held a number of different ministerial posts. Was one of those posts minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. I was minister for the interior from February 1993 to October 1997. In addition to that, I have been minister for health, I'm minister for research, I'm minister for ecclesiastical affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And focusing on your time as minister of the interior, was your work connected to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, to a very great extent. We received 20.000 Bosnian refugees in Denmark, and it was a major task for us both in terms of logistics but also, of course, in terms of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you left the ministry -- your position as minister of the interior in 1997. Why did you leave your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: It had nothing to do with the Bosnian refugees or the policies pursued in relation to them. The reason was a more fundamental disagreement concerning the long-term immigrant policy, disagreement between the prime minister and myself, and for that reason the logical consequence was that I left my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And very briefly, what was your position in respect to the refugees at that time?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I was in charge of a policy which was not to be too rigid as regarded the reception of the refugees, and in addition to that I was to pursue an inclusive policy concerning the integration of the refugees who were given permit to stay in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Have you written any books that are relevant to the region, to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've written two books. One is particularly relevant in relation to this case. It's called "Witness of Madness," and it concerns the situation in the north-western part of Bosnia, among other places, and I co-wrote it with a university lecturer by the name of Karsten Fledelius, who is from Copenhagen university. He's an historian. He speaks the language, the local language, that is, and he studied at the university of Beograd when he was young.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Were you in the north-western part of Bosnia in November 1996?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was there even before then. I was there in June 1996, and I returned a couple of months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And where in particular were you at that time, in November 1996?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I was in Kljuc and in the area, the nearby area of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, in case it is of assistance, Kljuc is referred to on pages 17 and 18 of the Prosecution's municipality map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, you've referred to your trip to Kljuc in November 1996. What was the original purpose of that trip?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, the original purpose of my trip was that in my capacity as minister of the interior, I was going there to inaugurate a number of buildings that Denmark had donated to the municipality of Kljuc. They were buildings intended for refugees from the area, refugees staying in Denmark but who wanted to go back very quickly, and it was to provide a shelter for them, because the vast majority of the buildings in the villages around the town of Kljuc were completely destroyed and that was why they needed to have a place to live while they were building their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And briefly, what could you observe of Kljuc in November 1996?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, Kljuc, the town of Kljuc, was like a ghost town. There were no people there, or very few people, that is, almost no cars in the street, and almost all the shops were closed. And the reason for this was that the entire Muslim part of the population had been cleansed away in 1992 and 1993. And later in 1995, the Serb part of the population -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I've asked the witness to repeat it, because there was a person in the booth disturbing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can repeat my answer. The reason why the atmosphere was very ghost-like was that the majority of the population had simply fled the town in 1992 and in -- and in 1993 the Muslim part of the population was thrown out, and later when the area was recaptured, a major part of the Serb population fled the local area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what is the basis of the observations you've just made in respect to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, the basis was that in those days I moved around in the area to a great extent with the Major Hadic, and I was shown several villages in which there were basically not a single house intact, left intact. I was also shown how a number of mosques, I think there were about 12 or 13 of them in total, they had been destroyed. And if I recall it correctly, the number stated concerning the number of buildings destroyed in the area, well, that number's 6.387.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And approximately how many times have you been back to Kljuc since you were there in November 1996, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you the exact figure, but it's somewhere between 12 and 15 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And where were you on the 8th of November, 1996?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I was in Kljuc, as I said before. I was there to -- well, excuse me, what was the question? Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Where were you on the 8th of November, 1996?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I was in Kljuc, and as I said, I was there to inaugurate the buildings that had been donated by Denmark, and in this connection it turned out that I was also involved in the exhumation of one of the local mass graves, and I was involved in the identification of the remains of part of the male population from the small town called Biljani, which lies outside Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And why were you involved with that exhumation?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, on the trip down there from Denmark, we stopped over in Bihac and I had meetings with the OTA and UNHCR, and I was indirectly then invited to be the reliable witness from the outside who could then afterwards tell about what went on over those days, and quite exactly as I've been prepared to, the mayor, Hadic, he invited me to take part, and of course I did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart will now play a video in Sanction. This is 65 ter 28085A, and I note there are no words and there is no transcript, so I hope we can only play it once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, the woman that we saw on that clip with her hand over her mouth, who was that?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: That was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And where are you?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: That was out in the Laniste farm, which is a few kilometres outside Kljuc town. That was where several mass graves had been found, and this one was called Laniste 1, and here was found a very large number of human remains from Biljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you attend any other locations in connection with the excavation of the bodies from this mass grave?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on in the same day I took part in the identification, which took place in the grammar school gymnasium. The bodies had been laid out in rows, and the relatives then walked about trying to recognise their family members, and at the same time they were requested to identify objects that had been found on the bodies or that had been found lying around in the grave. And I should add maybe that this was before DNA technology had been taken into use in connection with such identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart will now play another video in Sanction, which is 65 ter 28085B. There are a few words in the final seconds of this video, so you might wish to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to rely on it, on the words?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We don't need to rely on the words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we do not rely on it, if we put the sound that includes now then the music low, then we don't have to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Birte Weiss: I was not prepared that we would -- that we would be asked to be present at such a thing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have explained to our Danish interpret what the situation is. Since we do not rely on the words, there was no need to translate them, but I have been unclear in this respect. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, you mentioned being at this school gymnasium and identifying the -- certain of the bodies. Is that what was happening in the footage that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do both of the clips that we have just watched accurately depict your attendance firstly at the Laniste 1 excavation and secondly at the -- at the Biljani school?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. They give a glimpse, which is a correct picture of what happened, but I was there over some days, so it was a lot more than just this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And briefly, you refer to a picture of what happened. What picture were you able to build up of what has happened?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, it was quite clear that it was massacre that had taken place and that the bodies from this massacre, that they had been thrown into a -- what I remember as a 20-metre deep cliff, and they were now dug out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You refer to a massacre. Were you told where that massacre took place?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender into evidence these two clips as the next public Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear no objections. Mr. Registrar, the two clips would receive what numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 28085A becomes Exhibit P515, and 65 ter 28085B becomes Exhibit P516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P515 and P516 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, did you again visit Kljuc in July 1999?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. I visited Kljuc, and this time I stayed for three weeks, starting in July and finishing in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And why did you visit Kljuc at this time?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I visited Kljuc because I had -- it had been decided that I should gather my impressions in the form of a book, and I went there to try to provide additional material and primarily to confirm or disconfirm a number of the both oral and written statements I'd heard about what had happened in Biljani in the three years that had passed since 1996. So it was to get an additional foundation of the book I had decided to write.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Specifically, what was your book intended to be about?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: That was to be about two things: First, a description of the refugee conditions in Denmark, and I chose a very specific refugee group, namely people who came from Bosnian Krajina and thus also Kljuc, et cetera. That was one purpose. And the other purpose was to describe what they were flying from. What were the events that took place that brought them to a foreign country and what led to the fact that they couldn't stay at home, in their home country.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And how did you obtain the material for this book?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I got it in many ways. As I mentioned before, there were a number of refugees from this area in Denmark, and I got in close contact with them. It was a larger group of people. And in addition, we collected -- we -- it's me and Karsten Fledelius that I mentioned before, we collected material on -- when we were there in 1999. But it was a process that stretched over three years, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart will now play another video, 65 ter 28085C in Sanction. This time I do rely on the words, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps also to inform the Danish interpret, we'll play this video the first time without translation. You are, however, invited to listen carefully and to check whether the transcript you have received is corresponding with the text spoken, and then we play it for a second time in which we expect translation to be there. Now, I've not been informed about the Danish interpreters. Will they interpret from English, that is, the English translation, the English interpretation as provided by the colleagues, or is it that the English words are spoken in the video-clip itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Danish words are spoken on the video-clip, among other words, and those are translated into English. We already have English subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, in the second round, the Danish interpreter is invited to interpret into English. Let's proceed with the first round of viewing and listening to the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will now play it again with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be -- we usually, and that's perhaps I've not been clear enough, we usually do not rely on the subtitles, but we usually work on the basis of the interpretation given in court of the words spoken, as I understand here, spoken in Danish. Could we play it again and hear the simultaneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Birte Weiss: The police in Kljuc were very helpful in relation to helping us in our hunt for Samardzija. One might say that they actually helped us to lay down a strategy for finding him. "Police chief: I told you that we found something -- some literature in the school, something that he had written. We can show you and you can read this. "Karsten Fledelius: You should show us some of the literary he wrote. We would be very interested in that. What did he write? "Police chief: This is the document where you can see the signature of Marko Samardzija."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, why was this footage recorded?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Part of our stay in Kljuc at that time, it was a week, we were followed by a Danish TV documentary crew who wanted to show how the work with such a book took place, and this is the reason why we today have some footage that shows the text of the documents -- of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The man in the video sat next to you with -- with the beard, who was that?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Mr. Karsten Fledelius from the Copenhagen university. He was acting as an interpreter for me, and he's also a co-author of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And just in a few words, the other two men in the room, who were they?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: The two other persons, the man at the end of the table is a local police, chief of police, Dafic [as interpreted], and the uniformed police officer to the right in the picture is Safaracic Smail [as interpreted] is his first name. And why I remember the names so well, these two police officers were extremely helpful in relation to our work of finding -- finding Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Who was Samardzija? Marko Samardzija is the name referred to on the footage.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Marko Samardzija was a schoolteacher in Sanica, a neighbouring city of Biljani. He was a very well-known person in the area. He is a Serb, and he was part of the set-up that had existed, as turned out later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, the Chamber has some concern about the way in which this testimony goes and the questions. We understood from the 65 ter summary that the witness could, and as she did, testify about the exhumation, but to ask the witness to give second, third, fourth-hand evidence on matters which she obtained, and I have no problem with her work and the book, but of course was obtained in a setting for which we do not know to what extent all sides were heard, et cetera. And to present that as evidence where we have quite a bit of direct evidence, that is of some concern to the Chamber, and the Chamber wonders what this adds. For example, that the policeman was very helpful in helping the witness in obtaining her information. I mean, if he would not have been helpful or if he would have been someone else, I mean that's all the probative value of that how important the work may have been to inform the public, but the probative value before this Court is limited if there is any at all. Would you please focus on matters of which the witness has first-hand knowledge as the exhumation and the way in which bodies were identified and that objects belonging to persons were identified rather than to ask the witness to tell us about what she learned from others about persons at a time where she was not present in the area. Mrs. Weiss, I hope that you do understand that this does not in any way mis-appreciate the importance of your work, but of course your work in writing books is different from what we do in court, that that is in an adversarial setting hearing the testimony of witnesses primarily about what they observed, saw themselves. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply answered the questions I am asked, and I was asked about this and that was why I answered the question. But I'm willing to elaborate on everything that has to do with the exhumation and identification procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you did not misunderstand me. It was in no way criticism that you answered the questions. It was, rather, Mr. Jeremy reminding on what he is expecting to do in this courtroom to assist the Chamber. I appreciate not only your work but also that you answered the questions to the best of your abilities. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as noticed in our 65 ter summary, this -- this witness interviewed Marko Samardzija. And that interview followed shortly after the footage we just saw. In that interview certain documents are -- were referred to by Marko Samardzija. Those documents we'll now look at, and they were provided to this witness by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we then have is not a hunt for Mr. Samardzija, but you will put documents to the witness, and you'll ask questions about what the witness learned herself from Mr. Samardzija during that interview. That falls within the scope of what we expect you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, in the -- Mrs. Weiss, in the video footage we saw, we saw the police make reference to certain documents they say were authored by Marko Samardzija. We'll take a look at some of those documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask Ms. Stewart to bring 65 ter 28087 to our screens. Your Honours, Ms. Stewart just reminded me I've not tendered the video-clip we just watched, 28085C. I'd like to tender that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the third video-clip played today. Mr. Registrar -- or Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object to this video since there is no relevance in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lack of relevance. It will marked for identification under what number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The video is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy. You'll have an opportunity later to explain the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, do you recognise the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I was -- it was shown to me at the police station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And are you aware of who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. If you go down on the screen and move the text, you can see that it was written by Marko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd also ask -- I'd like to move to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we see that, please? Could we move that document such that ... Yes. Now we have the signature there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to another document, 28088. If we could call that up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Weiss, do you recognise this document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it, and I saw it on the same occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And very briefly, do you know what these documents were about?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not understand the original language, but they have been translated for me, and they, very briefly, are about the necessity if you're a Serb in that local area of preparing for a showdown with the Muslim part of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you know who these documents were circulated to?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, they were first and foremost sent to Marko Samardzija's soldiers. He was a captain of the first degree, and it was a kind of a message to his troops, but I've also been told that they were also distributed to a slightly broader group locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Marko Samardzija himself told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender those two documents as the next Prosecution public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 28087 becomes Exhibit P518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted -- no, not yet. We'll first hear from Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second document that the witness elaborated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at this moment dealing with the first one. Could we limit ourselves to the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First one, I think it's not sufficient to just recognise the signature. If the document, the contents of the document is not discussed, we don't think it's sufficient enough to introduce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's first --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to this witness. Maybe we can -- it can be re-introduced through bar table, but not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would not object against bar tabling it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If -- when it comes through the bar table then we would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would then deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- deal with that, but through this witness it's not sufficient enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let us first ask the witness. You were asked about whether you had seen this document before. You gave an answer when you saw it. You were then asked about who the author was. Now, apart from -- you said you saw the -- it was Mr. Samardzija. We could see that his signature is on the document. Was it ever confirmed that he authored and signed this document in any other way than by looking at this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, confirmed by whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whomever. By himself, by someone else, by experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the police in Kljuc sent the documents as part of material they had collated and which they had passed on through the court in Bihac to the war Tribunal, and that meant that they were in no doubt whatsoever about the authenticity of this document. The reason why there was no doubt about it -- another reason was that they were found shortly after the war at -- on Marko Samardzija's desk in the school in Cerniska [as interpreted]. He simply had not taken them with him when he fled the premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the police told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. I think the Registrar had given a number already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's Exhibit P518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Marked for identification. The second document of which, Mr. Jeremy, I think you have not shown us the second page, but it's on the second page that the name of Mr. Samardzija appears and is where we find a signature. Mr. Lukic, you said you had objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The same objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same objections. Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number so that it could be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 28088 becomes Exhibit P519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Weiss, what you were told about the origin of this second document, is that the same as what you were told in relation to the first document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the distribution of this document, I think you said that you knew about the distribution because Mr. Samardzija had told you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whether the word "distribution" is the right word, I shouldn't be a judge of that, but it was primarily made for his soldiers. But in addition to this, among the Serbian part of the population, they had gotten knowledge about it and as much he confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you, in his presence, looked at these documents and he explained for whom they were meant to be sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
