utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We didn't look at the documents when we visited Marko Samardzija, but we went on asking whether he had written some documents to -- before the massacre. He first was reluctant, said he hadn't written anything that could excite the population, but the -- during the two and a half hours conversation, he nevertheless remembered that he might have written something that had been left in his office at the school and that he had not taken with him when he fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, you've referred to on a number of occasions your interview with Marko Samardzija, and I'd now like to show some footage of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll ask Ms. Stewart to play in Sanction 65 ter 28085D, and there are some words in this clip, so it will be need to play twice, but I'll cut down the original amount of footage I was intending to show. I'll just show a minute or so, but I'll ask Ms. Stewart when to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll play it first to check on the words spoken, and then the second time we'll receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll now play it for a second and we'll receive interpretation. It stopped at 48:50, and we now start again at 47:25.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Marko Samardzija: Well, people say different things. "Birte Weiss: Well, it's exactly because people say so many different things that we have come. We want to hear from you what happened the way you saw the situation. "Marko Samardzija: Let me tell you, there was an order that some of the most extreme national fascists of Muslim nationality should be sent to Manjaca. I said at the time that I thought there were about 14 in our area. In my opinion, those were the 14 extremists. The rest should not be touched. "Karsten Fledelius: Fourteen extremists. Don't touch the rest of the people he said at the time. Then who gave your -- did he give the order himself? "Marko Samardzija: Before the action, before the action the Muslims were to be taken to the school on the evening of July 9. "Karsten Fledelius: ... of the seventh month, July."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, of the footage that we just watched of your interview with Marko Samardzija, there was a reference to a meeting on the 9th of July and a reference to orders being given on the same date. Do you recall Marko Samardzija talking about these things?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that the Court Officer bring 65 ter 03063 to our screens. This is an order given by a Lieutenant-Colonel Drago Samardzija, dated 9 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss -- Mrs. Weiss, do you recognise the order on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This was shown to me at the police station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you know who Lieutenant-Colonel Drago Samardzija was?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, I was told, but I don't know much about military ranks and their description. Therefore, I don't want to go into details about who had a right to give orders to their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And who were you told this person was?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I was told this by the two chiefs of police at the police station in Kljuc, and Marko Samardzija also mentioned the name Drago Samardzija during the conversation I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: What did Marko Samardzija say about the name Drago Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact words spoken, but this came up in connection -- what we saw on the screen, that he mentioned the 9th of July, and he said some orders had been given, and it was in connection with a meeting that took place [indiscernible] prior to the massacre on the following day. The meeting took place in Sanica and there was a fair number of leading officers of different ranks who were present, and it was in this connection that he also mentioned Drago Samardzija. Marko Samardzija was also present at the meeting himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this exhibit, 65 ter 03063, as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would object, Your Honour, since this witness cannot confirm neither who wrote it nor the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the origin, could you express yourself on that? She said she saw it shown to her at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- we think that the police officers cannot confirm the origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The document will be marked for identification. Mr. Registrar, under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 03063 becomes Exhibit P520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed. Mr. Jeremy, at the same time I'm looking at the clock, and I'm wondering whether -- where we are as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I probably have about 15 more minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That goes then beyond your estimate. You asked for one hour and a half finally, I think, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but then we received some more documents, and I think that if we go beyond this point in direct, we'll have to keep this witness for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just have a look now. If we take a break now, we would then be at quarter past 12.00 until quarter past 1.00. We would have a little bit over one hour and a half. Mr. Jeremy, is there any chance that you would be able to finish more in line with the estimate you gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll do my very best, Your Honours, and I'd also like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if Mr. Jeremy would need another seven to eight minutes, would that do? We would then have for you I think one hour and 40 minutes approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do our best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 12 .18 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Jeremy, the Chamber has carefully monitored the examination-in-chief and grants you another seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed. I'll be very strict on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the video that we watched at the end of the last session, 65 ter 28085D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It becomes Exhibit P521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P521 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, in the video footage we watched just before the break, we saw Marko Samardzija refer to 14 extremists in connection with the events on the 10th of July, 1992. What specifically did he say about those extremists?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I tried to have a precise definition of what he meant by "extremists." We were told layers in his explanation. One was more general. It was people who -- who were a danger to the Serb part of the population. That was point number one. And point number two, it was young men from families, young men from families who didn't have clean hands in 1941 when there was a massacre in precisely the same local area but with the Serbs as victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were these extremists identified in any particular way in the event -- preceding the events of the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: He -- in the interview he talked about -- that he knew precisely who they were, because as a schoolteacher in the area, as a prominent person, he had a very detailed personal knowledge of the persons in the area. So in his head, he had an idea of who they were or who he were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did others have an idea of who these people were on the eve of the 9th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I wasn't present, so I have no possibility of answering this question precisely, but it was said by Marko Samardzija that there were lists of citizens who -- who had to be brought or taken to the school in Biljani where they were to be registered, and there were considering more on that list than the 14 that he considered as extremists. I cannot give you a more precise answer, because as I said, I wasn't present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to call up Exhibit 65 ter 2797B and this is an extract of Mrs. Weiss's book, "Witness To Madness." In particular I'd like to go to e-court page 3, and I'd like to -- excuse me. Yeah, e-court page 3 in the English, halfway down the third paragraph, and in the B/C/S, e-court page 4, halfway down the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many pages is the extract, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's six pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for clarification of the record, it's 27976B. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Page 3 in e-court in the English, halfway down the third paragraph, and page 4 in the B/C/S. Sorry, in English it's page 3, halfway down the third paragraph. Page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registrar tells us that there's only one page in e-court, which surprises me, because when I look at my e-court version, I have six pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have six pages B/C/S version, and one page English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have six pages in English, Mr. Registrar. You'll find the page at a later stage. Put the question to the witness to the extent possible, Mr. Jeremy, because you have not much time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, in your -- in your book, "Witness To Madness," you quote Marko Samardzija as saying to you the following in respect to the events on the 10th of July, 1992: "It didn't help either that I called the Commander-in-Chief and told him what was about to happen in Biljani. 'Shove off, go home,' he just said. That was at 9.00, and there were as yet no dead on the road, all those terrible things I first heard about later." Mrs. Weiss, did Marko Samardzija told you -- tell you who he called? Did -- specifically the name of who he called?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: He mentioned that he contacted the people he could get in touch with. He created the impression that he -- both on the spot, that he objected on the spot, and he mentioned the name Jovo Kevac. And in addition, by telephone he contacted several people whom he wanted to tell what was going on in Biljani in those hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did he tell you who those several people were or what office they occupied?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: He said that they were the commanding people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I'm sorry, but I told you before we would be very strict in time. We're not going for three, four, or five minutes, ask the witness to stay here over the weekend. Again we have monitored carefully your cross-examination. I made already a few comments. Would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in your examination in chief, of course. I misspoke. Could you wind up in the next minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Could I call up in e-court 65 ter 19966A. This is a record of an individual leaving Kljuc specifying the particular property to be left behind, dated the 10th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, do you recognise or have you seen similar documents to the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do recognise this document, and I have seen several similar documents. It was customary that in order to get on a convoy out of Kljuc, for people who had to flee the town, they would have to sign such a declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- again, you invite or let the witness tell us what happened at the time. The witness can tell us about the document. She has no personal knowledge. She may have researched it but has no personal knowledge of that. I pointed to that several times. Where, Mrs. Weiss, did you see this and similar documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document I saw at the police station in Kljuc, and subsequently in the months and years after that I've seen similar documents in local authorities. That would be the town hall of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you want to tender it, the Chamber will consider it to be MFI'd depending on Mr. Lukic's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do object to -- for this document to be introduced through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to tender it, Mr. Registrar, what would the number be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be P522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P522 is marked for identification. Mr. Jeremy, this [overlapping speakers] time is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I have one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We said we would be very strict. If there's any time left at the end that one question can be put if Mr. Lukic doesn't use all of his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, this is not the usual way of ending an examination-in-chief, but you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Weiss.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter didn't get this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mrs. Weiss. [Interpretation] Well, today we will have a strange combination of languages, but I'm happy that we will be able to include Danish also today in the courtroom. I can see that you have had quite an impressive career, of course, and it's an honour to have such a prominent person as yourself before us here today. However, your expertise mostly concerns Denmark and Danish society. So in my question, what I would like to put to you is this: Is it correct that you are not an expert on relations in Yugoslavia and Bosnia, particularly regarding the historical and the political aspect?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- you can become an expert many different ways. My path towards gaining knowledge was that as previously mentioned, I was minister for the interior in the period, or most of the period during which war was waged in Bosnia. In that connection, I had to gain in depth insight into developments in Bosnia, and I had to do so because the events here -- or there, rather, why crucial in determining the number of refugees coming to Denmark shortly after the individual events. And because of that, I had on a daily basis to read reports from the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs and also UN documents, and I also followed the international media. So it's correct that I don't have an education in this field, neither as regards history and not in terms of language specifically. I only speak the language in -- very mediocrally. But in a professional context I also, for reasons of necessity, collected knowledge about matters that were crucial in relation to our reception of refugees in Denmark, and that included specific events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may have noticed that the Chamber has tried to focus the evidence of this witness very much to fact she knew and has intervened several times on that. So therefore you may have understood this. Apart from the content of the testimony of the witness which was not very expert-like to say so, why now explore what is not her expertise where we tried to do our utmost best to keep the Prosecution within the limits of a witness of fact? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Weiss, today you testified about the role of Marko Samardzija in these events. Is it correct that you received information that he had received this assignment from Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic was, as far as I know, the leader of the military police in Kljuc. I do not recollect exactly what he said about the various both military units and police units competencies in relation to the military units. I said in my answer to the Prosecutor that I don't have any in depth specific knowledge about military ranks and the competence associated with the individual officers' ranks and how they are inter-related, so I can't answer your question in any way that is different from the answer I gave to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, perhaps matters are simpler than they look at first. The simple question was whether you received information that the assignment of Marko Samardzija was given to him by Vinko Kondic. Did you hear about that, apart from who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was -- that was the simple question. Mr. Lukic will now put his next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you allow me to give a reason for my inability to confirm this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know, you confirm it. If you do not know, it doesn't need a reason. It's good as it is. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to ask you something about how people acted in that area at the time. We will be going through your book to see if you had any information about this crime, this incident, having occurred for reasons of revenge. So can we please look at 65 ter 27976 in e-court, please. Page 18, please. In the English, fourth paragraph from the bottom. Obviously I don't have the same pages in e-court as those shown here. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 18 in e-court, Mr. Lukic, is page 17 in the English hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the fourth from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say in the book, speaking about Marko Samardzija, we can see that at the top of our screens. In the first paragraph, you said: "...he mentioned the name of the neighbour who killed his father 58 years ago ... he started to shake when he spoke about this, how all the men and boys over the age of 12 at that time were taken prisoner and executed." Now we will need to look at page 27. The first paragraph of the same document. This might be a mistake then. Can we look at page 25, please. I apologise. Page 25 of the English version, please. You say: "For him personally, it was a question of revenge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We cannot see the reference. We don't know where Mr. Lukic is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are reading. Interpreters have difficulties in finding it. At this moment we have e-court page 26 on our screen for the English, and for the B/C/S we have -- could you verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need the next page in English, page 26 on the bottom, but before it was discrepancy for one page. Can we move one page up. First paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now looking at page 27 in e-court, page 26 in the English hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked for 27th page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] I will read it again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see line 2, the sentence begins: [In English] "For him personally, it was a matter of vengeance. His father had been killed in 1941 by a group of Croats and Bosniaks, and at his mother's death a few years ago, he complained at the funeral that she had not been able to witness 'the vengeance of his despicable murder.'" [Interpretation] My question to you is this: Did you find out from others that you spoke with that Marko Samardzija and armed local Serbs acted out of vengeance?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I believe that one should be very careful when generalising. I certainly want to stick to what Marko Samardzija actually said, and -- and he used this as a supplementary reason, and part of this reason was that he had experienced that his father, when he himself was five years old, that his father was a victim of the massacre that is mentioned in 1941, and he supports this further by referring to the fact that extremists are, among others, those who did not have clean hands in 1941. So there is a logical connection in his statement, but I do not want to generalise in relation to other persons who were involved in that massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question has been misunderstood, if it's well translated. If you look at the English, Mr. -- you asked whether the witness found out from others, that means through other sources, she consulted other sources show spoke with, whether, as I understand your question, whether they confirmed that Marko Samardzija acted out of vengeance. Could you tell us, because part of your answer was, Mrs. Weiss, that what he told you. Could you tell us whether this was confirmed by other sources? You are looking at Mr. Lukic. It's difficult for you to know who puts the question, but I did. Could you confirm that there were other sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were two parts in the question of the Defence. One of the aspects was a concrete aspect concerning Marko Samardzija. The other aspect of the question was whether one would consider that there were other persons in the area that also acted on the basis of vengeance, motive. My answer is that I can only relate to what Marko Samardzija himself said and what others said in this connection, and this was that there was a vengeance motive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so I will not allow myself to assess what other people meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, first of all, if I ask you to stop, would you please do so. Second, you continue to give your answers on the basis of a wrong understanding or a wrong interpretation of the question. The question was not whether others acted out of vengeance. The question was whether you only heard from Mr. Samardzija that he acted in relation to what had happened to him personally in the Second World War, or that others told you the same about Mr. Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, okay. Now I think it's clear to me what I'm being asked. Well, I knew this from Marko Samardzija, and a number of those other very many people that we were in contact with at the time, they had the same view, meaning they said that in the case of Marko Samardzija, there was a vengeance motive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you hear from others, Muslims, that you spoke with that other Serbs also acted out of vengeance?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: That's the question that I -- well, that's what I said just a minute ago, that it's difficult for me to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm asking you anybody of the people, such as Nasiha and other people that you spoke with, did they tell you anything in this regard? Did they or not? If yes, can you please tell us who it was that told you something like that and when?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, you need to specify what you mean about in this context, in this relation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- I'll rephrase the question now. Did you hear from any other person you spoke with that others, other Serbs than Marko Samardzija, had acted out of vengeance? We're not asking your opinion about whether they did. We're only asking you whether other Muslims told you that apart from Marko Samardzija, other Serbs also acted out of vengeance, whether this was told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our sources were not only Muslims. There were also a number of Serbs who have contributed and been -- and whom we have interviewed in connection with the book. We got the impression that it was very characteristic of Marko Samardzija, but that this could also be more widespread, this vengeance motive. But I cannot give you any names or references to what concrete persons who acted on the basis of a vengeance motive apart from what I've said about Marko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have any concrete names of those you interviewed who gave you this impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We spoke to, I believe, something like a hundred different persons in connection with our work on this book. It's 13 years ago. I could mention a few names, but I -- I don't think it's correct to be specific about what other persons in a third party view might have of vengeance motive, but as one of our interviewees in connection with the book, I could mention Skrago Savancic [as interpreted]. He was a member of the Municipal Council in Kljuc. He didn't go into any interpretation of how this vengeance motive should be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll leave it further in your hands, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you hear from people whom you interviewed that the people who committed the abuse, the mistreatment, were frequently drunk?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you also hear that Serbian units had problems with discipline among the speedily assembled and frequently insufficiently trained soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, it appears from one of the declarations that we have seen from Marko Samardzija that he had to express himself also in writing. He had to express himself to his soldiers in such a way as to discipline them. So the answer to the question must be that these soldiers had been gathered in a short time and that there might be disciplinary problems, but apparently they were, nevertheless, able to undertake the work that they were told to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we now look at page 36, please, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thirty-six in e-court, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page 35 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Weiss, paragraph 4, line 2, which states: [In English] "There are many examples of how the guards in the camp took the most gruesome vengeance on old wrongs, maybe all the way back to a fight during their school days or some disagreement on basis -- on a business matter. This ethnic struggle which suddenly arose was used as a cloak for --" We lost the page. We need page 36 in e-court. " ... which suddenly arose which was used as a cloak for brutality, pettiness and greed." [Interpretation] Is it therefore correct that you had heard from people whom you questioned there were a lot of cases of vengeance disguised by combat, and also there was greed under the guise of combat?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Page 36 does not refer to Biljani massacre. This refers to an interview with a refugee in Denmark who's called Mihanovic, Sulejman Mihanovic [phoen], and he gives a long interview about this. He expressed that this was how he perceived it in his area. He's from Kocavac [as interpreted] close to Prijedor. This is how he understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it had nothing to do with Biljani. We'll move on. Now I'm going to ask you something about the Samardzija case before the court of Sarajevo. I have found in documents that you followed the trial of Marko Samardzija, which was conducted in Sarajevo court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard some of the Pale case. I lived for one year in Sarajevo, and this coincided with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By following the trial [Danish on English channel] outcome both in judgement and appeal stages, you know that Marko Samardzija was not convicted of the murders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: That's correct. It was only part of the indictment that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Bosnia-Herzegovina court in Sarajevo, he was convicted of unlawful imprisonment of civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the trial, did you find out that the civilians who had been picked up in Biljani were handed over to the police?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Well, I was under the impression that they were given or handed over to the representatives of the army and the police. Both parties were present at the school in Biljani where the men were transferred, but it's true that police was an important part, the police was an important part of the entire team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, now we go to the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only one more question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, the buses that were used to transport people from Biljani to Kljuc or the buses that set off towards Kljuc, is it correct that the only escort provided was that of the police?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me, Your Honour. I was just checking when our break is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The break will be in approximately 15 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to ask you now about the Serbs of Kljuc after the war. You met Zdravko Stevandic. Who was that man?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: He was a local classman. He was a member of the municipality of Kljuc, and also in the period when he lived in Banja Luka, because he didn't think there was any foundation for -- for returning, which he did later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked on the reconciliation project; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: It wasn't I personally -- worked on that project in Kljuc, but I took part in forming some reconciliation projects, and I saw to it that the first financing of these projects was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After 1996, you visited Kljuc between 12 and 16 times according to what you told us. What did you learn? How many Serbs returned to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: The first period after the war, not very many returned, but among other things, because of hard work from Marko Stevandic [as interpreted], there were families in the villages who started returning, but they had a difficult time adjusting, and some of them moved away again. And today the population in Kljuc is quite -- is dominated by Bosniaks. It means only a small percentage of Serbs and an even smaller percentage of Croats. I would like to add that might make it even more understandable. At the Dayton agreement, Kljuc municipality was split into two. This means that Kljuc itself and the villages we have talked about so far, they were on the Bosniak part, and right on the other side of the Dayton line a new municipality Riplek [as interpreted] was set up. This is then only the Serb population living here. So when I'm talking about Kljuc municipality after the war, then it's the part that became the Bosniak part. The other part is on the other side of the sector border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the other side of the separation lines only a few villages from the Kljuc municipality remained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: It's not a very -- it's not as big as the part located on the Bosniak side; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know today who committed the murders in Biljani?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Do I know that personally? It's not my job to determine that. It's the job of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you reviewed a number of military documents. We are not going to go into each and every one of them. Is it true that you're unable to comment on the contents of the document and the military justification of the orders contained in those documents?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: [In English] Have you -- have you finished your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I think I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I -- what Mr. Lukic asked you was whether you're unable to comment on the contents or on the possible military justification for the orders described therein. Are you able or are you unable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said previously, I have no in depth knowledge of the various ranks in the military hierarchy, but of course I can comment on the documents if the Court wants me to do so. I would be willing to comment on the contents of the order. There's no problem in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- you are encouraged to do that only if you have any personal knowledge about the order or the content of the order. To comment in journalistic terms is not what we expect you to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I have read the order that is referred to, and my reading of it is that this is the way in which the individual units were instructed regarding the specific assignments they were to perform on the 10th of July from 5.00 a.m. That way of reading it, there's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Weiss, looking at your film, I noticed on the Muslim tombs or headstones that are shown in this film, that there is an inscription which reads "Sahid." Is it correct that the word "Sahid" means a fallen combatant?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: My knowledge of the Bosniak language is not well enough for me to go into any detailed definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your research and in the interviews that you conducted, did you find out anything about the fighting that was going on between the Muslim and Serbian forces from the late May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, on the 28th of May, there was a Serbian raid against a neighbouring town of Biljani, Vecici. The local people tried using ordinary hunting weapons to resist, but they didn't stand a chance against this overwhelming military power that eradicated the town, and for that reason it ended up with something very similar to the occurrence in Biljani, and that is that the men were taken to the school, in this case in Vecici, and they were killed, all of them. However, later on it turned out that a couple of witnesses had survived. And I spoke to one of those witnesses, and I was given a very detailed description of what happened, and this is also stated in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know for how long Vecici resisted the Serb attacks? Do you know that the fighting went on for six months?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about that. I know that the massacre that took place at the school in Vecici was over very quickly, and I haven't heard of any major and comprehensive combat action for a long time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have heard evidence in this Tribunal, therefore, I'm not going to burden you with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. It is time for a break. Could I invite you not to challenge what is not in evidence. I mean, it's clear that this witness wasn't there at the time. Therefore, there's better evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This question was obviously my mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This question was obviously my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also not to -- what is not tendered from the book of course doesn't need to be challenged unless you find anything in the book which of course would support your own case; in that case, in cross-examination you have some latitude to deal with those matters. Could I ask you where we are in terms of time after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will reorganise myself, and I don't think that I have much left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Weiss, we take a break of 20 minutes. You'll be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Mr. Groome, the Chamber received an e-mail about an inflexible witness this Chamber in all its flexibility doesn't know how you become so inflexible, but if you want to call him in the first week of February, then the Chamber will be able to hear his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think our inquiry was what week we would be off so we could schedule witnesses. Given the pattern we're working, whether we're taking off the first week or the second week of February when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not decided yet, but we are so flexible and so accommodating that if that witness cannot come at any other time, the Chamber will hear his evidence in that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think the Chamber misunderstood the e-mail. It is not about the witness being inflexible it's just that to schedule witnesses, we just need to know when we are sitting. That's all it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought there was a very special reason here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's not further deal with the matter at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you're ready to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. And I have gone through my questions and I have only one area left, very small area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would need 65 ter 27976. That's the book. Page in English version 4, paragraph 3. Actually, in B/C/S version, page 4, paragraph 3. In English version, page 2, paragraph 8. We have to add one page. So in English it's page 3. We made page 2 from the book. In English version we need paragraph 8. Starting with "None," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Weiss, in your book you said: "None of the parties to the Bosnian war were merely villains or merely victims. There were prison camps, expulsions and the burning of houses in every part of the country. However, it was mostly Bosniaks who came to Denmark and it was they who suffered the greatest loss of human life, property and prospects for the future. This book makes use of their point of view and makes no pretence of being a value-free historical account." [Interpretation] Would you say today as well that your intention was not to be impartial?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: When I put it in this way in the book, it's also to draw attention to the fact that the greater part of the sources used in the book are Bosniaks. That's partly due to the fact that the greater part of the refugees that came to Denmark were Bosniaks, although there also were Serbs and Croatians, but the Bosniaks were the greater part. But something that you cannot get from this formulation in the book is that the book should be siding with one or would be partial to one side. I would describe the book in this way: It was a collection of the best knowledge that was available in 1999. It was the knowledge that was available with the sources that we had access to from all three population groups. Obviously, later on a great many details and connections have been revealed, also in other court cases also concerning the Kljuc area. The court case against Stakic and Breznic [as interpreted] and several others. So you have to read this to mean that here I am communicating the knowledge available at the time when the book was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness now carefully explained why your question was wrong. Your question was: "Would you say today as well that your intention was not to be impartial?" That could not reasonably read from the portion you read to the witness, but the witness has better explained than I could do it that your question was misinterpreting the book. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were writing the book, is it correct that you used the Bosniaks' point of view and that you did not mean for your book to be an impartial historical record, as we can find that written in your book?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: It's only true to the extent that the greater part of the sources used in the book are Bosniaks, but it appears very clearly that another significant person in the book is Marko Samardzija, who is a Serb and who was much involved in what happened in Biljani. So to say this -- called this partial in a negative sense, that I believe is not great.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How would you call it, impartial -- partial in a positive sense? Partial in a positive sense?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I don't know what this means, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] The translation we got: "So to say this," something "called this partial in a negative way -- sense." Something's missing from the transcript. [Interpretation] And did you not also say that you would not allow yourself to be Teflon coated, preventing you from being objective?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: It's correct that in the documentary film I use this expression involving Teflon, but that's in a different connection. That's in connection with the general impression that a minister naturally gets when he suddenly is responsible for 20.000 refugees from an area where the worst imaginable things happen. And I also use this expression as a sort of explanation for the fact that in addition to my professional work, I have also later on been involved in conditions in Bosnia. I've been involved in the further cross-ethnical peace process which is characterised by the fact that both Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs take part in this in Kljuc. So this is general comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My last question: Is it correct that you lobbied in Denmark in favour of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: No, this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Weiss, thank you very much. These are all the questions I had for you, and I would like to thank you for answering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any need for re-examination? I'm not saying to finish your examination-in-chief, but re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour. No need for any re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you. Mr. Lukic did put to you, page 27 in e-court of 65 ter 27976, that is the excerpt of the book where at the top of that page you explained that Mr. Samardzija's father was killed and that revenge may have played a role in his acts. Now, I understood that this is what you learned from Mr. Samardzija himself and that you had similar information from others. Now, in the page immediately preceding the last lines are and I'll read them to you, "For him," and I'm referring to e-court, page 26, hard copy page 25, "For him," and you were referring to Samardzija after you had explained his position as the company commander, you wrote: "For him, it was an inevitable war about creating a 'Greater Serbia.' His task was complete extermination." When you wrote that down, was that also on the basis of what he had told you, or was the basis for it information you received from other persons? And I take it that it's just an impression you gained on the basis of the sources I'm now asking you about.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: This page was not shown on the screen, but I think I can answer your question without having seen it. I understood it was a referral to Samardzija's own attitude towards the vengeance motive, and what he described in connection with the 1941 incident was -- the job was to -- everybody above 12, big boys and men, in this local area were supposed to be exterminated because they were Serbs. I don't know if this is what you referred to, but I didn't see the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, we have the text on the screen, 27976, e-court page 26. Now, my question was not about what his attitude was but on what basis you gained this impression.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Can I get the correct page, please? It's page 26 in the English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have hard copy page 25, e-court page 26. That's the same, and you find it at the very end of the page, last paragraph, starting with, "We don't know whether Marko Samardzija himself shot anyone." You then referred to his position as a company commander. And I was focusing on the last lines which I read to you: "For him, it was an inevitable war about creating a 'Greater Serbia.' His task was complete extermination." I did not invite you to explain what you meant there, but I was asking you whether you gained this impression on the basis of your conversation with him or from any other source. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: Okay. I have now seen the real text -- or the correct text, so I can now answer the question. It was the impression we got partly through interviews with -- with him. It lasted two and a half hours. And the impression we gained from a number of other sources that we talked with both during our stay in July, August, but also a number of interviews with sources that we were in touch with in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you able to identify those sources or are you not specifically on this element? If you can, please do so. If you cannot, tell us.

utterances.speaker: BIRTE WEISS
utterances.text: I have it as a general impression. We could call it the sum of all the information we got, but in addition, some of the persons that I gather would also have to appear in court as protected witnesses. We have also talked with these witnesses or these persons, and it would be more relevant that it's their statements than my statements that apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have my questions triggered any need for further questions? If not, Mrs. Weiss, this then concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I would wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. Groome, when I said something about inflexibility, I meant to inflexibility after a date had been set. In the e-mail it says: "Once we book him, he will not be able to alter his dates." That's the only thing I referred to as part as inflexibility is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, I would like to use the time remaining to deliver a decision on the admissibility of the Philipps report. The Chamber will now address the admissibility of the Philipps report, the component parts of which remain marked for identification; that is, P451, two organisational charts; P452; and P453, the latter being explanatory notes; P454, which is an alphabetical list of units and formations; and last, P455, alphabetical list of personnel. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution requested that the report be marked for identification pending the conclusion of Witness Philipps's testimony, and the Defence indicated on the 9th of November, 2012, that it maintains its objections to the report's admission raised in its written submissions of the 20th of February, 2012, the 6th of March, 2012, and the 26th of March, 2012, all submissions on the Prosecution Notice of Disclosure of the Philipps report under Rule 94 bis. The Chamber recalls that in its 1st of November, 2012, Decision on Defence Motion to Disqualify Richard Philipps as an Expert and Bar the Prosecution from Presenting his Report, the Chamber addressed the Defence objections to the admission of the Philipps report. The Chamber nevertheless deferred ruling upon its admission to give an opportunity to the Defence to fully explore its challenges to the report's reliability in cross-examination, particularly as regards Witness Philipps's methodology and sources. Having heard the evidence of Witness Philipps, especially in relation to the sources used and the methods applied, the Chamber considers that the objections to the reliability of the Philipps report are unfounded and that it bears relevance and probative value meriting admission into evidence under Rule 89(C) of the Rules. Exhibits P451, P452, P453, P454, and P455 are hereby admitted into evidence, and this concludes the Chamber's decision. If there are -- are there any further procedural matters to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could I ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We adjourn, and we will resume on Monday, the 19th of November, quarter past 2.00 in this same Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of November, 2012, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
